propositions.text: This is the judicial review of the denial of the Applicants’ refugee appeal by the RAD under section 110 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
propositions.quote: This is the judicial review of the denial of the Applicants’ refugee appeal by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD], pursuant to section 110 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (SC 2001, c 27) [the Act].

propositions.text: Applicants are a married couple from Jamaica fearing persecution by JLP supporters for refusing to vote for the party in 2011 elections.
propositions.quote: The Applicants, Rajiv and Tamara Dowansingh, are a married couple from Jamaica fearing persecution by supporters of the Jamaica Labour Party [JLP] because they refused to vote for the party in the 2011 national and local elections.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of the Applicants' refugee appeal denial; the Applicants fear persecution in Jamaica for not voting JLP.

propositions.text: The RAD upheld the RPD's rejection of the claim, finding no palpable and overriding errors in RPD's credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The RAD upheld the rejection of the claim by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD], concluding that there were no “palpable and overriding errors” relating to the credibility findings by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker, RAD, upheld the RPD's rejection of the claim, finding no palpable and overriding errors in credibility findings.

propositions.text: The court finds the RAD’s decision reasonable and dismisses the judicial review.
propositions.quote: For the reasons below, I find the RAD’s decision [Decision] to be reasonable, and dismiss the judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's decision reasonable and dismisses the judicial review.

propositions.text: Applicants are Jamaican citizens who did not vote in the 2011 national or local elections.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of Jamaica who did not vote in the national election in Jamaica in December 2011, or the local election in March 2011.

propositions.text: Applicants allege their neighborhood was controlled by JLP gangs who lost elections to PNP.
propositions.quote: They allege that the neighbourhood in which they lived was beset by organized gangs associated with the JLP, which had lost the elections to the People’s National Party [PNP].

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say they are Jamaican citizens who did not vote and allege their neighborhood was controlled by JLP gangs who lost to PNP.

propositions.text: Mr. Dowansingh claims he was attacked by JLP thugs in November 2012 for not voting, and police took no action after his report.
propositions.quote: Mr. Dowansingh claims that in November 2012, he was attacked by JLP thugs for failing to vote, thereby helping bring the PNP into power. He allegedly reported the incident to the police, but no action was taken.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Dowansingh claims he was attacked by JLP thugs for not voting and police took no action after his report.

propositions.text: The RPD found several material irregularities in the Applicants’ narrative undermining their credibility.
propositions.quote: At first instance, the RPD noted several material irregularities in the Applicants’ narrative which undermined their credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found material irregularities in the Applicants' narrative undermining their credibility.

propositions.text: Applicants made two visits to Canada before claiming refugee status, delaying claim until January 2014 after third entry.
propositions.quote: For example, the claimants obtained Canadian temporary visas which they used to visit Canada from October 9-26, 2012, and March 22-April 14, 2013. The second visit, notably, came after the supposed attack on Mr. Dowansingh, but a refugee claim was not made until January 2014, a month after arriving in Canada for a third time.

propositions.text: Applicants remained in the same house and district after second trip despite danger and having family elsewhere and means to relocate.
propositions.quote: Further, when the Applicants returned to Jamaica after their second trip in April 2013, they did not relocate until their latest entry into Canada in December 2013. Rather, the Applicants remained in the same house in the same district in which the assault had taken place, despite having immediate family living in other districts and sufficient financial means to remove themselves from danger (Application Record [AR], p. 50-51).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Applicants delayed refugee claim after visits and stayed in dangerous area despite means to relocate.

propositions.text: RPD found police letter submitted by Mr. Dowansingh untrustworthy due to lack of signature, file number, poor printing, and post-dated claim.
propositions.quote: Mr. Dowansingh also submitted a police letter documenting the alleged assault he suffered in November 2012, but the RPD determined that this was “not a trustworthy document” for several reasons (AR, p.53). The document did not contain an original ink signature, did not contain a file number, the crest appeared to have been printed by an ink jet printer and the document’s date post-dated the e refugee claim (AR, p. 50).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the police letter untrustworthy due to signature, file number, printing, and date issues.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD erred by applying 'palpable and overriding error' standard to review of RPD’s conclusions.
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ argument that the RAD’s Decision was unreasonable rests on the following premise - the RAD erred by applying the standard of intervention of “palpable and overriding error” to its review of the RPD’s conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the RAD erred by applying the 'palpable and overriding error' standard to review RPD's conclusions.

propositions.text: RAD should have independently assessed genuineness of police letter; failure tainted credibility findings.
propositions.quote: More particularly, the decision maker should have conducted an independent assessment of the police letter submitted by the Applicants, and decided independently whether it was genuine. The fact that the RAD did not do so tainted the remaining credibility findings, as the RAD’s view of the Applicants’ narrative may have taken a different tone had it believed in the veracity of the November 2012 assault.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD should have independently assessed police letter's genuineness; failure tainted credibility findings.

propositions.text: RAD must independently assess genuineness of documents and not defer to RPD on such matters.
propositions.quote: I will begin by acknowledging that the genuineness of a document must be independently assessed by the RAD. The RAD should not defer to the RPD’s conclusions on such matters, because the RPD is in no better a position to assess these documents than the RAD (Njeukam v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 859 at para 14; Kurtzmalaj v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1072 at para 35; Sow v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 295 at para 13).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must independently assess document genuineness and not defer to RPD on such matters.

propositions.text: Despite using 'palpable and overriding error' standard, RAD independently assessed police report and found RPD's concerns reasonable.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding the RAD’s use of the standard of “palpable and overriding error” in its review of the entirety of the RPD decision, the RAD appears to have examined and come to an independent assessment of the police report for itself: [19] “….the RPD did not accept the police report as being trustworthy, due to the numerous inconsistencies within the body of the report and the quality of the report in general. The RPD, in its reasons, cited clearly the concerns it had when looking at the police report. The RAD has reviewed the evidence in this area concerning the police report, where the RPD found it to be riddled with anomalies, and those were identified clearly in its reasons; as such, the RAD finds the RPD finding regarding the value of the police report to be reasonable in this circumstance.” (AR, p.11, emphasis added)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD independently assessed police report and reasonably agreed with RPD's concerns despite standard used.

propositions.text: More detailed RAD reasons on personalized documents and country conditions increase likelihood of court finding independent assessment.
propositions.quote: As a general practice, the more detail the RAD can provide in its reasons about its thoughts on the most salient issues pertaining to personalized documentation and country conditions, as well as including country condition evidence and whether it agrees with or differs from the RPD’s assessment, the more likely a reviewing Court is to find that such evidence was independently assessed by the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states detailed RAD reasons on documents and country conditions help courts find independent assessment.

propositions.text: RAD is not required to detail all independent conclusions if RPD's findings are numerous, obvious, and well-articulated.
propositions.quote: However, this does not mean that the RAD is confined to a mechanistic process in which it must detail how it arrived at all of its independent conclusions. Where the RPD’s factual findings are numerous, plainly obvious, and well-articulated, as is the case here regarding the authenticity of a document, then the RAD’s succinct acknowledgment of these concerns may be enough to demonstrate that it has conducted independent assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD need not detail all independent conclusions if RPD's findings are numerous and well-articulated.

propositions.text: If RPD's conclusions involve specialized expertise or novel findings, RAD must detail how it reached its conclusions.
propositions.quote: At the other end of the spectrum, if the RPD’s conclusions turn on other discrete observations, specialized expertise, and/or novel findings, then there is a greater need for the RAD to detail how it reached its conclusions on the evidence. In such cases, merely stating that the evidence was examined and concurring with the RPD may not reflect that an independent assessment has actually been conducted (Cepeda-Guiterrez v Canada (Minster of Citizenship and Immigration), 157 FTR 35; Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 500 at para 9; Mestre v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 375 at para 15; Shahini v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 211 at para 15).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must detail conclusions if RPD's findings involve specialized expertise or novel findings.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed evidence and shared RPD's concerns about police letter authenticity; no need to repeat RPD's words.
propositions.quote: In this case, the RAD explicitly stated in its reasons that it reviewed the evidence regarding the police letter, and noted the RPD “identified clearly in its reasons” that the letter was “riddled with anomalies”. In the context of this case, I take this to mean that the RAD reviewed the evidence and had the same concerns as the RPD regarding its authenticity. There is neither any point nor requirement to parrot the words of the panel in arriving at the same credibility-based findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD reviewed evidence and shared RPD's concerns about police letter authenticity without repeating RPD's words.

propositions.text: RPD's credibility conclusions rested on more than police letter genuineness; RAD found no palpable and overriding errors in credibility assessment.
propositions.quote: In any event, the RPD’s conclusions regarding the Applicants’ credibility rested on more pillars than merely the genuineness of the police report submitted. The RAD found “there is [sic] no palpable and overriding errors relating to the credibility assessment by the RPD” and that “[t]he RPD considered the Appellants’ delay in departure, their travel to Canada, and their re-availment to Jamaica. It concluded that their actions speak to a lack of subjective fear” (AR, p.11).

propositions.text: RAD held negative credibility findings extended to section 97, affecting both subjective and non-subjective fear concerns.
propositions.quote: The RAD further held that the negative credibility findings made by the RPD extended to section 97, as they went “not only to subjective fear, but also to the non-subjective fear concerns”.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's credibility conclusions rested on multiple factors; RAD found no palpable errors and extended findings to section 97 fears.

propositions.text: Negative credibility findings under section 96 may affect claims under section 97; separate section 97 analysis would not materially differ here.
propositions.quote: I find the RAD’s conclusions to be reasonable. Negative credibility findings made under section 96 may also affect the validity of a claim under section 97, even though subjective fear is not part of the assessment for the latter section (Mahadeva v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 415 at para 15). While the RPD could have performed a separate section 97 analysis, it would not have made a material difference.

propositions.text: Applicants’ behaviour seriously undermined credibility, justifying findings applicable to both sections 96 and 97, obviating need to consider section 97 claim.
propositions.quote: Specifically, I agree with the RAD that the Applicants’ behaviour, including their delay in making a claim and their re-availment to Jamaica, as well as implausibilities and inconsistencies in their narrative, so seriously undermined their overall credibility that these findings were applicable to both section 96 and section 97. The negative section 96 credibility finding obviated the need to consider the claim under section 97 (Restrepo Mejia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration); 2010 FC 410 at para 20; Reza Gorostieta v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 343 at para 32; Nyathi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1119 at paras 21-24; El Achkar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 472 at paras 38, 43-44).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds negative credibility findings under section 96 affect section 97 claims; Applicants' behaviour seriously undermined credibility.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD erred in applying 'palpable and overriding error' standard to RPD’s credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the RAD erred in assessing the RPD’s credibility findings on a “palpable and overriding error” standard.

propositions.text: Certain case law holds 'palpable and overriding error' is the correct standard for RAD to review credibility findings.
propositions.quote: I begin by noting that certain case law holds this is indeed the standard of intervention on which the RAD should review credibility findings (see for instance, Spasoja v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 913 at para 40).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD erred applying 'palpable and overriding error' standard; court notes some case law supports that standard.

propositions.text: Huruglica case holds RAD may respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not limited to intervening only on palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: In what has become the pre-eminent case on the standard of intervention by the RAD, Justice Phelan in Huruglica v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 799 at para 55, concluded that the RAD may “recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility” but is not limited to “to intervening on facts only where there is a ‘palpable and overriding error’.” I endorsed this approach in Brodrick v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 491 at para 34.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Huruglica case holds RAD may respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not limited to intervening only on palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: The RAD should have been less deferential to the RPD's credibility findings in this case.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the RAD should have been less deferential to the RPD’s credibility findings in this case.

propositions.text: The RAD should have recognized and respected the RPD's credibility determinations, not reviewed them for palpable and overriding errors.
propositions.quote: The RAD should have “recognized and respected” the credibility determinations by the RPD, not reviewed them for “palpable and overriding errors”.

propositions.text: The RAD was unaware it could intervene when the RPD made a non-obvious or non-crucial error in credibility determinations.
propositions.quote: In other words, the RAD wasn’t aware that it could have intervened in circumstances where the RPD made an error in a credibility determination which wasn’t obvious (palpable) or of crucial importance (overriding) (Canada v South Yukon Forest Corporation, 2012 FCA 165 at para 46).

paragraphs.summary: The applicants argue the RAD should have been less deferential to the RPD's credibility findings and recognized errors beyond palpable and overriding ones.

propositions.text: RPD's credibility conclusions warrant some deference based on testimony.
propositions.quote: This Court has repeatedly held that RPD’s conclusions on issues of credibility based on testimony clearly warrant some measure of deference (Denbel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 629 at para 31; Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 500 at para 8; Ngandu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 423 at para 31).

propositions.text: Due to inconsistencies and implausibilities in the Applicants' narrative, no reviewable error exists in the RAD's decision not to intervene.
propositions.quote: As a result of the numerous inconsistencies and implausibilities in the Applicants’ narrative, I fail to see a reviewable error in the RAD’s Decision not to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's credibility findings deserve deference and sees no reviewable error in the RAD's decision given applicants' inconsistent narrative.

propositions.text: No basis exists to return the matter for reconsideration despite applicants' arguments.
propositions.quote: Despite the very able arguments of counsel for the Applicants and best efforts to convince me that the matter needs to be returned for reconsideration, I see no basis upon which to do so.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I, therefore, dismiss this application for judicial review.

propositions.text: There are no questions for certification.
propositions.quote: There are no questions for certification.

propositions.text: No award as to costs is made.
propositions.quote: There is no award as to costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review, denies reconsideration, and makes no certification or cost awards.
